extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political institutions; general readers of political science and U.S. constitutional history
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and normative account of U.S. State politics and the Territorial form of government: how parties and factions form, how State political life has changed, the structure/powers/limitations of Territorial government, and the process and conditions for admission to statehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis of state party formation
rubrics_metrics.description: All these groups or factions were or are associated on the basis of some doctrine or practical proposal which they put forward. But it sometimes also happens that, without any such basis, a party is formed in a State inside one of the regular national parties; or, in other words, that the national party in the State splits up into two factions, probably more embittered against each other than against the other regular party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes parties/factions formed from substantive doctrines or practical proposals (examples: Granges, Farmers' Alliance, People's Party, Prohibitionist party) from purely personal or leader-centered factions (examples: Hunkers and Barnburners; Stalwarts and Half-breeds; Regular and Union Republicans). Use these categories to analyze the origin and durability of state political groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor-party influence strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prohibitionist party... acts chiefly by influencing the existing parties, and frightening them into pretending to meet its wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor parties may have little legislative representation but can shape policy by pressuring major parties; evaluate a minor party's effectiveness by its ability to influence major-party platforms or to make them adopt its doctrines rather than by seat counts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of decline in State politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignity and magnitude of State politics have declined. They have become more pacific in methods, but less serious and more personal in their aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include more personal rivalries, fewer large ideological struggles, less public-spirited engagement with State government, and political battles fought primarily at polling booths or in vote-counting rooms rather than in broader civic mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of reduced State prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: This change... is due to that shrivelfing up of the State... the facilities of communication, the movements of trade, the unprecedented diffusion of literature, and... the dominance of the great national parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing changes in the salience of state politics, consider structural forces (communications, trade, media diffusion) and party system centralization that draw attention toward national politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter engagement pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: The average American voter... troubles himself little about the conduct of State business. He votes the party ticket at elections as a good party man... The politics which the voter reads by preference are national politics; and especially whatever touches the next presidential election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate citizen attention by observing whether voters prioritize partisan loyalty and national contests over local/state legislative matters; consider issue-specific engagement (e.g., canal management, railway rates) as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and strategy of reform-minded citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Some public-spirited young men have... thrown themselves into the muddy whirlpool of the New York legislature, chiefly for the sake of carrying Acts for the better government of cities... With the help of the press they were able to carry measures such as an improved Ballot Act, or Civil Service Act, or an Act for checking expenditure at elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform efforts may succeed through sustained individual commitment, media support, and targeting specific institutional reforms; however, structural rules (e.g., representation restricted to one's district) can impede maintaining a lasting reforming party in the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for national arena for reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who... put them to the wheel, generally prefer to carry their energies into the field of national politics, thinking that larger and swifter results are to be obtained there, because victories achieved in and through the National government have an immediate moral influence upon the country at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding where to direct reform efforts, weigh the potential for quicker, broader impact via national institutions versus incremental local/state change; historical tendency favors national arena for perceived efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive empowerment tendency (Governor initiative)
rubrics_metrics.description: One is the tendency to turn from the legislature to the Governor and encourage him to take the initiative and assert himself as a motive power leading the legislature and appealing directly to the people for their support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern tendencies include widening the Governor's practical authority (though not necessarily legal functions) to overcome difficulties of diffused responsibility in large representative bodies; evaluate reforms that increase executive initiative as responses to perceived legislative weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of referendum and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of those highly democratic institutions, the Referendum and the Initiative... give evidence of the desire which is spreading in the West for the people to take power out of the hands of the legislature and wield it themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct-democratic devices are adopted where distrust of legislatures is strong; anticipate a learning curve and potential mismatches between popular expectations and what legislation can deliver; consider risks of oversimplification and need for citizen skill in lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and trigger for Territorial status
rubrics_metrics.description: When, with the westward advance of the whites, any particular region became sufficiently settled to require a regular government and be capable of some form of self-government, its boundaries were set, and it was erected into what is called a Territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use settlement/population thresholds and need for organized local government as criteria to determine when an area is made a Territory; historical practice tied Territories to paths toward eventual statehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental law of Territories
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental law of every Territory, as of every State, is the Federal Constitution; but whereas every State has also its own popularly enacted State Constitution, the Territories are not regulated by any similar instruments, which for them are replaced by the Federal statutes establishing their government and prescribing its form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Federal statutes (Congressional organic acts) as the equivalent of a constitution for Territories; they define institutions, powers, and limits in place of a locally enacted constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial executive composition and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive consisted of a governor appointed for four years by the President of the United States, with the consent of the Senate, and removable by the President, together with a secretary, treasurer, auditor... The governor commanded the militia, and had a veto upon the acts of the legislature, which, however, was (in most Territories) capable of being overridden by a two-thirds majority in each house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key markers: presidential appointment with Senate consent, presidential removability, specified term (four years), veto power subject to override, command of militia, obligation to report yearly and send messages to the legislature. Note propensity for the post to be used as party patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial legislature structure and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A Territorial legislature was composed of two Houses, a Council of twelve persons, and a House of Representatives of twenty-four persons, elected by districts. The session was limited (by Federal statutes) to sixty days, and the salary of a member fixed at $4 per day... The sphere of legislation allowed to the legislature was wide, indeed practically as wide as that enjoyed by the legislature of a State, but subject to certain Federal restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Territorial legislatures by composition, short statutory sessions, low pay, committee-driven business, residence requirements for members, and broad-but-restricted legislative competence; recognize Federal statutory constraints on specific subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory restrictions on Territorial legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative power of every Territory shall extend to all rightful subjects of legislation not inconsistent with the Constitution and laws of the United States. But no law shall be passed interfering with the primary disposal of the soil; no tax shall be imposed on the property of the United States, nor shall the lands or other property of non-residents be taxed higher than the lands or other property of residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Territorial laws, check consistency with the Federal Constitution and statutes; ensure laws do not burden federal property, interfere with federal land dispositions, or discriminate against non-residents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional supremacy over Territorial statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has the right to annul or modify by its own statutes any Territorial act. In some Territories every act was directed to be submitted to Congress for its approval, and, if disapproved, to be of no effect; in others submission was not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Congressional oversight as ultimate: Territorial statutes may be overridden, subject to varying procedural arrangements (explicit submission/approval or not). Historical examples include heavy intervention in Utah to break down polygamy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial judiciary composition and appeal routes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judiciary consisted of three or more judges of a Supreme Court, appointed for four years by the President, together with a U. S. district attorney and a U. S. marshal... appeals where the sum in dispute was above a certain value went to the Supreme Federal Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the Territorial judicial system by presidential appointments for fixed terms, mixed application of Federal and local law, practice/procedure regulated by Territorial legislature, and limited appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court in higher-value cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and citizenship rights in Territories
rubrics_metrics.description: The Territories sent neither senators nor representatives to Congress, nor did they take part in presidential elections. The House... admitted a delegate from each of them to sit and speak, but not to vote... His private or passive citizenship is complete: he has all the immunities and benefits which any other American citizen enjoys. But the public or active side is wanting, so far as the National government is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between full private civil rights of Territorial residents and the lack of political representation at the federal level; expect delegates to have speaking but not voting rights, and no participation in Electoral College/presidential elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and conditions for admission to Statehood
rubrics_metrics.description: When its population reached that of an average congressional district, its claim to be admitted as a State was strong... Congress, however, having absolute discretion in the matter, often used its discretion under the influence of partisan motives. The enabling act might prescribe conditions to be fulfilled by the State constitution, but did not usually attempt to narrow the right to be enjoyed by the citizens of the newly-formed State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission typically proceeds via acceptance of a constitution or an enabling act authorizing a constitutional convention; practical criteria include reaching a population comparable to a congressional district, economic stability, and occasionally specific enabling-act conditions (e.g., ordinances regarding religious toleration and public schools). Be aware of political/partisan influences on Congress's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling-act imposed irrevocable ordinances (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the cases of the Dakotas, Montana, Washington, Idaho, and Wyoming, the enabling act required the conventions to make 'by ordinance irrevocable without the consent of the United States and the people of the said States' certain provisions, including one for perfect religious toleration and another for the maintenance of public schools free from sectarian control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some enabling acts may demand specific, supposedly irrevocable constitutional provisions (e.g., religious toleration, secular public schools). Note the unresolved legal question ('quaere') whether such requirements would bind future state alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors considered for territorial fitness/state admission
rubrics_metrics.description: The descriptions of Dakota, Montana, Washington, Wyoming, Idaho, and Utah highlight area, climate, soil fertility, mineral wealth, population growth, and settlement patterns as factors bearing on future prosperity and suitability for Statehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess readiness for statehood by demographic measures (population size and stability), economic resources (agriculture, minerals, timber), geographic characteristics (climate, arability), and prospects for sustained settlement; historical admissions sometimes overlooked prudence for partisan advantage (example: early admission of Nevada).
